record.paper_title: Open Problems in Communication and Computation
record.original_question: What is the ultimate impact of algorithmic complexity on probability theory, and what is its relationship to information theory?

evidence.quote: Finally. what is the ultimate impact of algorithmic complexity on probability theory? And what is its relationship to information theory?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a finite binary string x ∈ {0,1}*, let K(x) denote its prefix-free Kolmogorov complexity, defined as the length of the shortest input to a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine U such that U outputs x. For an infinite binary sequence ω ∈ {0,1}^ℕ, say that ω is Martin-Löf random with respect to the uniform (fair-coin) measure if there is a constant c such that K(ω↾n) ≥ n − c for all n, where ω↾n denotes the first n bits of ω. Recall that the Shannon entropy of a discrete random variable X with distribution p is H(X) = −Σ_x p(x) log p(x), and that for computable distributions p on {0,1}^n one has the identity E_p[K(X)] = H(X) + O(log n).

Develop a comprehensive theory describing the ultimate impact of algorithmic (Kolmogorov) complexity on classical probability theory, and articulate its precise relationship to Shannon information theory. Concretely:

(a) Identify the largest natural class C of probability statements (e.g. almost-sure laws such as the strong law of large numbers, the law of the iterated logarithm, ergodic theorems, martingale convergence theorems) for which the classical "almost surely" can be replaced by "for every Martin-Löf random sequence" in a uniform effective manner, and characterize the obstruction for statements outside C.

(b) Determine the exact quantitative correspondence between Kolmogorov complexity K and Shannon entropy H beyond the known O(log n) coincidence on computable sources: in particular, give a meaningful interpretation of K-based quantities (algorithmic mutual information I(x:y) = K(x) + K(y) − K(x,y), algorithmic sufficient statistics, the algorithmic minimal sufficient statistic) as limits or refinements of their Shannon counterparts, valid for individual objects rather than ensembles.

(c) Decide whether there is a single unified framework subsuming both classical probability theory and algorithmic information theory in which entropy, complexity, randomness, and typicality are aspects of one underlying invariant.
artifact.status_search_result: The question, posed as a broad foundational research direction about the role of Kolmogorov complexity in probability and its links with Shannon information theory, remains open in the sense that no definitive unifying theory has been established. Substantial progress has been made — e.g. Vovk, V'yugin, Shen, Bienvenu, Gács, Hoyrup, Rojas and others have shown that many classical almost-sure laws hold for every Martin-Löf random sequence, and the algorithmic vs. Shannon information correspondence has been deeply studied (Grünwald–Vitányi, Vereshchagin–Vitányi) — but the "ultimate impact" remains an active program rather than a closed chapter.

status_evidence.title: Grünwald & Vitányi, Shannon Information and Kolmogorov Complexity
status_evidence.snippet: Compares Shannon information theory and Kolmogorov complexity, showing close correspondences and key differences.
status_evidence.claim: The relationship between Kolmogorov complexity and Shannon entropy has been partially clarified but is still being developed.

status_evidence.title: Bienvenu, Hoyrup, Shen — Algorithmic randomness and probability theory
status_evidence.snippet: Surveys how algorithmic randomness yields pointwise versions of probabilistic almost-sure theorems.
status_evidence.claim: Significant partial progress shows many almost-sure theorems lift to statements about every Martin-Löf random sequence.
